PURPOSE: Reduce enemy Influence in a country.

CONDITIONS: Opponent must have Influence markers in the target country.

COST: 1 card.

PROCEDURE: Each player rolls a die and each player adds the modifiers (listed below) to their own die roll. The high roller may remove the difference between the rolls from the opponent's Influence in the target country. Ties are considered a draw, and no markers are removed. A player may make several realignment attempts against the same country using the Operations points from the same card.

MODIFIERS:
+1 for each controlled adjacent country
+1 if adjacent to rolling player's superpower
+1 if rolling player has more influence in target country than opponent

<margin-right=12em><indent=1em>The</indent> Chinese Civil War space is considered adjacent to the Soviet Union and only the Soviet Union. The space is considered to be in Asia, but not South East Asia. It does not affect any scoring card. The only action that may be taken on the Chinese Civil War space is the placement of Influence Points by the Soviet player. The US player may not use Operations or events of any kind to effect the Chinese Civil War space. Once the Soviet player has placed 3 Influence Points</margin> on the Chinese Civil War space, it has no further effect. The markers may be returned to the Soviet player’s pool, and the Chinese Civil War space is ignored for the remainder of the game.

<indent=1em>The</indent> Soviet Union must place three Influence on the Chinese Civil War space to Control it. Soviet Influence is placed in the Chinese Civil War space according to the rules for placing influence in countries. If the China card remains unclaimed throughout the game, no player receives the victory point for possession of the China Card during end game scoring.

<indent=1em>Until</indent> the Soviet Player has placed 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space, the China Card is in no player’s possession. Once the Soviet player had placed 3 Influence Points into the space, the player immediately receives the China Card face up and ready for play. Additionally, the ban on play of the Red Scare/Purge and Formosan Resolution events is immediately lifted.

<indent=1em>Until</indent> the Soviet player has placed 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space, the Soviet player may not play Red Scare/Purge nor Cultural Revolution as events. Additionally, the US player may not play Formosan Resolution as an event. These cards may be played for Operations Points normally.

Special US Condition: For the purposes of playing Ussuri River Skirmish or Nixon Plays the China Card as events, the US is deemed to be in possession of the China Card if the Soviet Player has not yet placed the 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space.
Until the Soviet Player has placed 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space the Russian player subtracts an additional 1 when rolling for the resolution of the Korean War event.
Events made unplayable or restricted due to these Event Restrictions are still playable for Operations points.
Military Coup
<color=white>PURPOSE:</color> Reduce enemy Influence in a country and possibly add Influence for your own superpower.
Components
<color=white>CONDITIONS:</color> Opponent must have Influence markers in the target country.
<color=white>COST:</color> 1 card.

<color=white>PROCEDURE:</color> the Stability Number of the target country is multiplied by two (x2).  A die is rolled and added to the Operations points on the Coup triggering card.  If this modified die roll is greater than the doubled stability value, the coup is succesfull, otherwise it fails.
<color=white>MODIFIERS:</color> None.

<color=white>SUCCESSFUL COUP:</color> the number of Influence removed from your opponent's target country is equal to the number produced by the Coup resolution.  If there is insufficient opposing Influence to remove, friendly Influence is added to make up the difference.
<color=white>UNSUCCESSFUL COUP:</color> No Influence markers are moved.
<color=white>MILITARY OPERATIONS (MilOPS):</color> the Required Military Operations marker is moved a number of spaces equal to the Operations value of the card.
<color=white>DEFCON:</color> any Coup attempt in a Battleground country degrades the DEFCON status one level to DEFCON 1.

<align="justified"><color=red>EXAMPLE:</color> The US player plays a 3 Operations card to conduct a coup attempt in Mexico. The US player has no Influence in Mexico; the USSR player has 2 Influence points.
<margin-right=7em>First the US player adjusts their marker on the Military Operations Track to show that they have spent three points on Military Operations this turn.

The map is divided into six Regions: Europe, Asia, Central America, South America, Africa, and the Middle East. Europe is divided into two sub-regions, Eastern and Western Europe. Asia also contains a sub-region, Southeast Asia. The country spaces that comprise a region share a map color, and sub-regions have shades of the same color.

Any event, rule, action, or card that refers to “Europe” or “Asia” includes the associated sub-region. Each space on the map represents a country or bloc of countries, and each country has a Stability Number representing that country’s overall stability, independence and power. Battleground countries operate the same way as normal countries, but have special rules for scoring and coup attempts. Their country name is highlighted in red for easy recognition.
Then they roll the die for a 4 and adds their Operations Number (3) to get a 7. They now subtract twice the value of Mexico’s Stability Number (2x2=4) from this result to get a final total of 3.
<margin-right=7em>This is the number of Influence markers they may remove from/add to Mexico. First, the US would remove the 2 Soviet Influence markers, then place 1 USInfluence marker.
Defcon & </allcaps>Mil<allcaps>Ops
The DEFCON Track

<indent=1em>DEFCON</indent> status measures nuclear tension in the game. The DEFCON level begins the game at its maximum ‘peace’ level of 5. It can go down and back up due to events and actions by the players, but if, at any point, it decreases to 1, the game ends immediately.
<indent=1em>The</indent> DEFCON status may never Improve above 5. Any event that would Improve the DEFCON status above 5 has no DEFCON effect.

<indent=1em>If</indent> DEFCON 1 status is reached, nuclear war breaks out and the game ends immediately. The phasing player is responsible for the status marker moving to DEFCON 1, and loses the game.

<color=red>EXAMPLE:</color> The US player plays Olympic Games, and the DEFCON status is at 2. The USSR player boycotts the game. The DEFCON status is degraded to level 1, and nuclear war is triggered. The US player, as the phasing player, has lost.
<indent=1em>Any</indent> Coup attempt in a Battleground country degrades the DEFCON status one level.
<indent=1em>The</indent> consequences of the DEFCON status levels are on the DEFCON Track, and are reproduced here:

Countries that do not share a border, but are considered connected, are shown via lines on the map. A country is considered to be Adjacent to all other countries to which it is connected. Each country on the map is considered either to be <color=white>Controlled</color> by one of the player's, or it is Uncontrolled. A country is considered <color=white>Controlled</color> by a player if the player has Influence Points in the country greater than or equal to the country’s <color=white>Stability Number</color>, and if the player’s Influence in the country exceeds their opponent’s Influence in that country by at least the country’s <color=white>Stability Number</color>.

•DEFCON 5: No effect
•DEFCON 4: No Coup or Realignment rolls are permitted in Europe.
•DEFCON 3: No Coup or Realignment rolls are permitted in Europe or Asia.
•DEFCON 2: No Coup or Realignment rolls are permitted in Europe, Asia, or the Middle East.
•DEFCON 1: Game over. The player responsible for the status going to 1 (the Phasing Player) loses the game.
PLAY NOTE: The region scoring button will display an icon to remind you that no Realignment or Coups are permitted.
DEFCON Icon
<indent=1em>Improve</indent> DEFCON Status Phase: At the beginning of any turn in which the DEFCON status is lower than 5, Improve the DEFCON status by 1.

<indent=1em>Improve</indent> & Degrade: In all cases, when the rules or cards indicate to ‘improve’ the DEFCON status, this means to move the DEFCON marker to a higher DEFCON number, while ‘degrade’ means to move the DEFCON marker to a lower DEFCON number.
Required Military Operations

By the end of each turn, each player must have played a certain number of Military Operations. Failure to do so results in a Victory Point penalty. The number of Military Operations required each turn is equal to the current DEFCON status number. If fewer Military Operations are carried out, your opponent gains 1 VP per unplayed Military Operations point. If both players suffer a Victory Point penalty, the net total should be implemented on the Victory Points Track.
<color=red>EXAMPLE:</color> At the end of the turn the US player has spent two points in Military Operations. If the DEFCON level is currently at 4 the USSR player would gain 2 Victory Points.
<indent=1em>Coup</indent> attempts and war events are Military Operations. Realignment Rolls are not considered Military Operations.

When Operations points are played in a Coup attempt, the phasing player moves his marker on the Military Operations track a number of spaces equal to the Operations value of the card. When a War Event card is played (e.g., Arab-Israeli War, Korean War etc.) the phasing player moves his marker the number of spaces designated by the event text.

Except for Scoring Cards, all cards contain an Operations Point value, an Event Title and Event Description. Scoring Cards are labeled “SCORING” and must be played sometime during the turn they are drawn. Cards with a Red star are only associated with the USSR, and cards with a White star are only associated with the US. Cards that have a split Red/White star are Neutral, and are associated with both sides.

Cards are played in either one of two ways - as Events or Operations. Many cards have an asterisk following their Event Title. When these cards are played as Events, they are removed permanently from the game. Cards that have their Event Title underlined, and are played as an Event, are in effect on the game board until they are cancelled. Cards that are discarded, but not removed from the game, are placed face up in the discarded pile.

<indent=1em>If</indent> a player uses a card for Operations points, and thereby triggers a War Event associated with his opponent, his opponent’s Military marker is moved on the Military Operations track as directed by the Event text.

<color=red>EXAMPLE:</color> The US player uses the ‘Arab-Israeli War’ card for Operations points, thereby also triggering the War Event (as it is associated with the Soviet Union player). In addition to the Event taking place as directed on the card, the USSR player moves his Military Operations marker two spaces on the Military Operations track.
<indent=1em>Events</indent> that allow a free Coup roll do not count towards required Military Operations.
Placing Influence
Quick Rules
<color=white>PURPOSE:</color> To increase Influence in a country.

<margin-right=7em><color=white>RESTRICTIONS:</color> All markers must be placed adjacent to, or in the same space with friendly Influence markers that were on the map when the Operations card was played.

<color=white>COST:</color> 1 Op Point to place an Influence marker in a country that is friendly-Controlled or Uncontrolled. It costs two (2) Op Points to place an Influence marker in an enemy-Controlled country.  If a country's Control status changes while placing Influence markers, additional markers placed during that action are placed at the lower cost.
<color=white>NOTE:</color> if any Ops points are spent for placing Influence, all ops points from that card must be spent on placing Influence markers.
Influence and Control Rules

The phasing player always decides whether the event is to take place before or after the Operations are conducted. If a card play triggers an opponent’s <color=white>Event</color>, but that <color=white>Event</color> cannot occur because a prerequisite has not been met, the Event does not occur.

Influence markers are placed one at a time. However, all markers must be placed with, or adjacent to, friendly markers that were in place at the start of the phasing player’s Action Round.

Exception: markers placed when required by an Event are not subject to this restriction, unless specifically stated otherwise on the card.

If the amount of influence is sufficent to gain control of the country, the Marker switches to either red for U.S.S.R. or blue for the U.S.A..

It costs one (1) Operations point to place an Influence marker in a country that is friendly-Controlled or uncontrolled. It costs two (2) Operations points to place an Influence marker in an enemy-Controlled country. If a country’s Control status changes while placing Influence markers, additional markers placed during that Action Round are placed at the lower cost.
<indent=1em>Influence </indent>markers may be placed in multiple regions and multiple countries up to the number of Operations Points on the card played.
<indent=1em>You</indent> may place Influence in any adjacent country you already have Influence in at the start of your placing Influence. Adjacent countries are highlight as below:
<indent=1em>Influence </indent>markers may always be placed in any country that is adjacent (connected) to the phasing player’s superpower space.

<indent=1em>Influence </indent>markers are treated like cash. Players may ‘break’ a large denomination into smaller denominations at any time. Additionally, the number of Influence markers included in the game is not an absolute limit. Small poker chips, coins or wooden blocks can be utilized to substitute in the event of a marker shortage.
Influence Marker
When a country flashes as below, you may add (or remove in certain cases) influence there.

For those of you who would like to dive right into the post-Quagmire era and try out the cool possibilities of a Landed Eagle, Star Wars, and Chernobyl, or Aldrich Ames, the Hostage Crisis, and Terrorism, here’s a scenario that cuts to the chase.

A sense of the game-turn structure is that the turns roughly represent the following years:

Thus, the Late War period would begin in 1975, say, with the Fall of Saigon. So it is that date (and a dose of interpretation of history into the TS fabric) that has been selected to set the influence and events for the opening of the Late War Scenario.

The US appears to begin the post-Vietnam era in a decidedly strong position in game turns. Whether or not the dominoes have fallen, the US still dominates Asia, for example. Play of the scenario has shown that a US Automatic Victory is well within reach, so the Soviet player in this scenario wins just for engineering a more graceful decline of the Socialist experiment.

Have fun, and please try to avoid The Day After…

Rules Summary
<color=white>PURPOSE:</color> Reduce enemy Influence in a country.
<color=white>CONDITIONS:</color> Opponent must have Influence markers in the target country.
USA / USSR Influenced
<color=white>COST:</color> 1 card.

<color=white>PROCEDURE:</color> Each player rolls a die and each player adds the modifiers (listed below) to their own die roll.  The high roller may remove the difference between the rolls from the opponent's Influence in the target country.  Ties are considered a draw, and no markers are removed.  A player may make several realignment attempts against the same country using the Operations points from the same card.

MODIFIERS:
+1for each controlled adjacent country
+1if adjacent to rolling player's superpower
+1if rolling player has more influence in target country than opponent
Example

EXAMPLE: The US player targets North Korea for Realignment. There are 3 USSR Influence points in North Korea, while the US player has none.

The US player has no modifiers—he does not control any adjacent countries and has less Influence in North Korea then the Soviets. The USSR player has +1 because North Korea is adjacent to the USSR and +1 for having more Influence in North Korea then the US.

The US player gets lucky and rolls a 5 while the USSR player rolls a 2 which is modified to 4. The result is the USSR player must remove one Influence point from North Korea.
Scoring

<indent=1em>The</indent> object of the game is to score Victory Points (VPs). Regional Victory Points are scored through geographic Influence over the six Regions. VPs can also be received through the play of certain Events. Each region has its own ‘scoring card’. Playing a scoring card causes Victory Points to be scored, based on how much influence each superpower has in that region at the time the card is played.
The following terms are used during Regional Scoring:
PRESENCE: A superpower has Presence in a Region if it Controls at least one country in that Region.

DOMINATION: A superpower achieves Domination of a Region if it Controls more countries in that Region than its opponent, and it Controls more Battleground countries in that Region than its opponent. A superpower must Control at least one non-Battleground and one Battleground country in a Region in order to achieve Domination of that Region.
USSR Controlled
CONTROL: A superpower has Control of a Region if it Controls more countries in that Region than its opponent, and Controls all of the Battleground countries in that Region.

Players score additional points during Regional Scoring, as follows:
•+1 VP per country they Control in the scoring region that is adjacent to the enemy superpower
•+1 VP per Battleground country that they Control in the scoring region.
•Victory points are then cumulated for both players, and the net difference between the two scores is marked on the Victory Point Track.
<indent=1em>Playing</indent> certain card Events may result in Victory Points being scored.
<indent=1em>Victory</indent> Points may be scored due to your opponent’s failure to perform the number of required military operations during the turn.
<indent=1em>A</indent> player may not be forced to Hold a Scoring Card through the effects of an Event(s).
PLAY NOTE: Trying to play scoring cards to coincide with your superpower’s peak influence in a region is often a crucial factor in winning the game.
<indent=1em>There</indent> are several ways to achieve an automatic victory in Twilight Struggle:

•The instant one player reaches a score of 20 VP, the game is over and that player is the winner. NOTE: All VP awards (for both players) that are scored during an event or scoring card must be applied prior to determining automatic victory.

•EXCEPTION: If a player reaches 20 VP during the Check Military Operations Status phase, proceed to the Reveal Held Card phase before declaring that player the winner. If the player who reached 20 VP is revealed to be holding a scoring card, then that player loses instead of winning.

•If either side Controls Europe, that side wins when the Europe Scoring card is played.

•Nuclear War: A player may also win the instant his opponent causes the DEFCON level to reach 1.

<indent=1em>End</indent> Game Victory. If neither side has achieved victory of any kind by the end of turn 10, then every Region is scored as if its regional scoring card had just been played (these new VPs are added to the current score). Southeast Asia is not scored separately: it is included in the Asia scoring calculations. Every Region’s score must be calculated before final victory is determined. Reaching 20 VPs does not result in Automatic Victory during scoring at the end of turn 10; however, Control of Europe does grant automatic victory to the controlling player, regardless of scoring elsewhere.

<indent=1em>Once</indent> all regions have been scored, victory goes to the player who has accrued most VPs. If the VP marker is on a positive number, the US wins; if the VP marker is on a negative number, the USSR wins. If the VP marker is on zero, the game ends in a draw.

<indent=1em>Operations</indent> points may be spent to attempt to move a marker to the next spot on the track. To do so, discard a card with an Operations point value equal to or greater than the number shown on the track into which you are attempting to advance. Roll the die: if the number falls within the range listed in the target box on the Space Race track, your marker advances to the new spot.

A player may only discard one card per turn in an attempt to advance in the Space Race. Exception: Space Race Track Special Abilities and certain Events may alter this one-card limitation, or advance the superpower's marker on the Space Race track.

<indent=1em>Advancing</indent> along the Space Race track results in an award of Victory Points, a special ability, or both. Five boxes on the Space Race track are marked with two numbers divided by a slash, e.g. Lunar Orbit has the numbers 3/1. The left-hand number is the amount of Victory Points awarded to the first player to reach that box; the right-hand number is the amount of Victory Points awarded to the second player to reach that box. Victory Points granted take effect immediately. All Space Race Victory Points are cumulative.

“We go into space because whatever mankind must undertake, free men must fully share . . . I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before the decade is out, of landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the earth.”
—John F. Kennedy
Special Abilities
Operations Point Value
<indent=1em>Special</indent> abilities are granted only to the first player to reach the space. The special effect is immediately cancelled when the second player reaches that box.
<indent=1em>The</indent> effects of these special abilities are immediate and cumulative.
Regardless of text on the card, an Event discarded to make a die roll to advance on the Space Race track is not implemented. The card is placed in the discard pile.
If a player reaches the final box in the Space Race, no more cards may be expended in the Space Race by that player for the remainder of the game.

<color=red>EXAMPLE:</color> The USSR player successfully reaches space 2. He may play a second Space Race Card during his next Action Round. If the USSR player reached space 4 before the US player had reached space 2, the USSR player could play two Space Race cards per turn, and require the US Player to show his Headline Phase event before selecting his own.

DESIGN NOTE: The Space Race is your ‘safety valve.’ If you hold a card whose Event is a good one for your opponent, and you don’t want the Event to occur, you can dump it on the Space Race (provided it has enough Operations points to qualify for an attempt to move forward).
Upon reaching space 2 (Animal in Space), the player is allowed to discard two Space Race cards per turn (instead of the usual one).
Upon reaching space 4 (Man in Earth Orbit), the opposing player must select and reveal his or her Headline Event before the player with a ‘Man in Earth Orbit’ makes his/her Headline Event selection.
Upon reaching space 6 (Eagle/Bear has Landed), the player may discard their Held Card at the end of the turn.
Upon reaching space 8 (Space Station), the player may play eight (8) Action Rounds per turn.
Event
Upon reaching space 2 (Earth Satellite), at the beginning of the Check Military Operations Status phase, add two Military Operations to the player's total.
Upon reaching space 4 (Eagle/Bear has Landed), once per Action Round, placing Influence in a country controlled by the opponent costs the standard 1 Operations point, rather than 2.
Upon reaching space 6 (Anti-Ballistic Missiles), once per turn the player may re-roll one of their Coup attempts, accepting the re-rolled result.
Upon reaching space 7 (Neutron Bombs), the player's opponent Coup attempts incur a -1 modifier to their die roll.
Basic Rules

“Now the trumpet summons us again — not as a call to bear arms, though arms we need, not as a call to battle, though embattled we are — but a call to bear the burden of a long twilight struggle...”

—John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Speech,
January 1961

<indent=1em>In</indent> 1945, unlikely allies slew the Nazi beast, while humanity’s most devastating weapons forced the proud Japanese Empire to its knees in a storm of fire. Where once there stood many great powers, now stood only two. The world had scant time to sigh relief before a new conflict threatened. Unlike the titanic conflicts of the preceding decades, this conflict would be waged primarily not by soldiers and tanks, but by spies and politicians, scientists and intellectuals, artists and traitors.

Twilight Struggle is a two-player game simulating the forty-five year dance of intrigue, prestige, and occasional flares of warfare between the Soviet Union and the United States. The entire world is the stage on which these two titans fight to make the world safe for their own ideologies and ways of life. The game begins amidst the ruins of Europe as the two new ‘superpowers’ struggle over the wreckage of the Second World War, and ends in 1989, when only the United States remained standing.

Twilight Struggle inherits its fundamental systems from the carddriven classics We the People and Hannibal: Rome vs. Carthage. It is a quick-playing, low-complexity game in that tradition. Event cards cover a vast array of historical happenings, from the Arab-Israeli conflicts of 1948 and 1967, to Vietnam and the U.S. peace movement, to the Cuban Missile Crisis and other such incidents that brought the world to the brink of nuclear annihilation. Subsystems capture the prestige-laden Space Race as well as nuclear tensions, with the possibility of nuclear war ending the game.

<indent=1em>Additionally,</indent> terms that have specialized meaning within these rules, such as ‘Influence’ or ‘Battleground’, are consistently capitalized to allude to their specialized context within the rules.
Asterisk = Remove from play if event is used
The Game Map

<indent=1em>The</indent> map is divided into six Regions: Europe, Asia, Central America, South America, Africa, and the Middle East. A region is a group of geopolitically connected nations, normally in close geographic proximity. Europe is divided into two sub-regions, Eastern Europe and Western Europe. Two historically neutral countries (Austria and Finland) are categorized as being in both Eastern and Western Europe. Asia also contains a sub-region, Southeast Asia. The country spaces that comprise a region share a map color. Sub-regions have shades of the same color.
<indent=1em>Any</indent> event, rule, action, or card that refers to ‘Europe’ or ‘Asia’ includes the associated sub-regions.

<indent=1em>Each</indent> space on the map represents a country or bloc of countries (hereafter simply called a country). Each country has a Stability Number representing the country’s overall stability, independence and power.
DESIGN NOTE: Although not exactly geographically correct, the Middle East includes Libya and Egypt for political purposes, while Canada and Turkey are included in the Europe Region.
Western Europe
Eastern Europe
Both Western and Eastern Europe
Battleground State
Non-Battleground State

Twilight Struggle has ten turns, and each turn will involve six or seven card plays by each player. At the beginning of the game, each player receives eight cards from the <color=white>Early War</color> deck. At the beginning of Turn 4, the <color=white>Mid War</color> deck is shuffled into the draw pile and the player’s hand size is increased to nine. At the beginning of Turn 8, the <color=white>Late War</color> deck is shuffled into the draw pile. When there are no cards remaining in the draw deck, the game reshuffles all discarded cards to form a new draw deck. The game will deal all cards remaining in the draw deck before reshuffling, except in Turns 4 and 8.

<indent=1em>Battleground</indent> States: Battleground countries operate the same way as normal spaces but have special rules for scoring and coup attempts. Their country name background is highlighted in red for easy recognition.

<indent=1em>There</indent> are two spaces on the map representing the geographic locations of the United States and the Soviet Union. They are out of play for Influence Markers, but provide the same benefits as “adjacent controlled countries” for the purposes of events and realignments.

<indent=1em>Countries</indent> are connected to one another via the black, red and brown lines on the map. Brown lines represent connections within a region. Red dashed lines represent connections between countries in different regions. The black lines indicate connections between countries and superpowers. A country is considered adjacent to all other countries to which it is connected.

DESIGN NOTE: Being adjacent is not entirely a reflection of geography. Several countries that share physical boundaries do not have connections in the game. This is not a map error but is part of the mechanics of the game and the political situation of the times.
<indent=1em>Controlling</indent> Countries: Each country on the map is considered Controlled by one of the players, or it is uncontrolled. A country is considered Controlled by a player if:

•The player has Influence points in the country greater than or equal to the country’s Stability Number, and
•The player’s Influence in the country exceeds his/her opponent’s Influence in that country by at least the country’s Stability Number.
EXAMPLE: To Control Israel (Stability Number 4), a player must have at least 4 Influence points in Israel, and must have at least 4 more Influence points in Israel than his/her opponent has.

<indent=1em>Some</indent> countries contain small numbers with blue or red backgrounds in the lower left or center-right portions of the country space. These numbers indicate Inluence points placed in that country at startup. Influence points that are assigned to a region, but are not assigned to a specific country are noted adjacent to the regional labels on the map.

<indent=1em>Except</indent> for Scoring Cards, all contain an Operations Point value, an Event Title and an Event Description. Scoring cards are labeled “SCORING” and must be played sometime during the turn they are drawn.
<indent=1em>Each</indent> card has a symbol to indicate which superpower is associated with its Event, as follows:

A turn in Twilight Struggle has the following game play steps:

A. Improve DEFCON Status
B. Deal Cards
C. Headline Phase
D. Action Rounds
E. Check Military Operations Status
F. The China Card
G. Turn Announcements

> A. Improve DEFCON Status : If the DEFCON level is lower than 5, the game will raise the DEFCON level by 1.

Twilight Struggle has ten turns. Each turn represents between three and five years, and will involve six or seven normal card plays by each player. At the beginning of the game, each player receives eight cards from the Early War deck. At the beginning of turn 4, the Mid War deck is shuffled into the draw pile and the players’ hand size increases to nine. At the beginning of turn 8, the Late War deck is shuffled into the draw pile.
<indent=1em>The</indent> Phasing Player is the player whose Action Round is currently being played.

<indent=1em>When</indent> there are no cards remaining in the draw deck, all discards are reshuffled to form a new draw deck. Note that cards played as Events with an asterisk (*) are removed from the game when they are played, and are not shuffled into the new draw deck.
<indent=1em>All</indent> cards remaining in the draw deck are dealt before reshuffling, except in turns 4 and 8.

<indent=1em>When</indent> moving from the Early War deck to Mid War, or from Mid War to Late War, the discards are not added to the deck—instead, the Mid War or Late War cards (as appropriate) are added to the existing deck and reshuffled. The ignored discards remain in the discard pile for now, but will be reshuffled into the deck in the next reshuffle.

C. Headline Phase

<indent=1em>Each</indent> player secretly selects a card from their hand. Once both players have made their choice, they reveal their cards to each other simultaneously. These cards are called ‘Headline cards’ and their Events take place in this phase (and if the event title has an asterisk, are removed from the game normally). To determine which Event takes place first, look at the Operations value on each card; that is its Headline Value. The card with the higher Headline Value takes effect first. In the event of a tie, the Headline Event played by the US player goes into effect first.

•Scoring cards may be played during the Headline Phase. However, they are considered to have a Headline Value of zero (0) and always take effect second. If both players elect a scoring card as their Headline Cards, the US player’s scoring card takes effect first.

•Players must create a Headline event, regardless of whether the event helps them or their opponent.

•‘The China Card’ may not be played during the Headline Phase.

•Unless the headline event specifically refers to availability of operations points, neither player receives operations points from cards played during the headline phase.

NOTE: If playing an opponent’s event during the Headline phase, your opponent implements the event text as if they had played the card themselves. However, the player of the headline card would be considered the phasing player for purposes of the DEFCON status.
D. Action Rounds

<indent=1em>There</indent> are six Action Rounds in turns 1 to 3 and seven action rounds turns 4 to 10. Players alternate playing cards, one per Action Round, for a total of six cards during turns 1 to 3, and seven cards during turns 4 to 10. The USSR player always takes his or her Action Round first, followed by the US player. All actions required by each card must be resolved before the next player starts his or her Action Round by playing a card. The player taking his or her Action Round is called the ‘Phasing Player’.

Intro

•Ordinarily, a player will have a card left over after the completion of all Action Rounds. This card is considered ‘held’, and may be played in subsequent rounds. Scoring cards may never be held.

•If a player has insufficient cards to take the requisite number of actions for the turn, that player must sit out of the remaining Action Rounds while the opposing player completes the turn.

Since this detracts from some elements of secrecy in the game, it is not necessary to use this rule in a non-competitive environment.

War Events

War Events: There are 5 “War” Events in the deck: Korean War, Arab-Israeli War, Indo-Pakistani War, Brush War, and Iran-Iraq War. These Events may be played regardless of the absence of either player’s influence points in either the attacking or defending countries. If there is no influence at risk in the war, the Event’s player still receives victory points upon success, and required military operations irrespective of success.

Influence Markers

<color=white>Influence Markers</color> are placed one at a time, and must be placed with or adjacent to friendly markers, that were in place at the start of the phasing player’s <color=white>Action Round</color>. It costs one (1) Operations point to place an Influence marker in a country that is friendly Controlled or Uncontrolled. It costs two (2) Operations points to place an <color=white>Influence Marker</color> in an enemy-controlled country. If a country’s Control status changes while placing <color=white>Influence Markers</color>, the additional marker's costs adjust accordingly for future placement for that <color=white>Action Round</color>.
Adjacent to Panama
Realignment Rolls

Realignment rolls are used to reduce enemy Influence in a country. Your opponent must have at least one (1) Influence Marker in the target country. Realignments are attempted one at a time and cost one (1) Operations point per attempt. Each player rolls a die and the high roller may remove the difference between the rolls from their opponent’s Influence in the target country. No Influence is ever added to a country as a result of a Realignment roll. Each player modifies their roll by:

> +1 for each adjacent controlled country
> +1 if they have more Influence in the target country than their opponent
> +1 if your superpower is adjacent to the target country
Coup Attempts

A <color=white>Coup</color> represents operations that change the composition of a target country’s government. A player attempting a <color=white>Coup</color> does not need to have any <color=white>Influence</color> Markers in the Country; however your opponent must have <color=white>Influence Markers</color> in the target country. To resolve a <color=white>Coup</color> attempt, the game multiplies the <color=white>Stability Number</color> of the target country by two (2), then rolls a die and adds the <color=white>Operations</color> points on the card to it. If the modified roll is greater than this target number the coup is successful. <color=white>Influence Markers</color> equal to the difference from the target country target number are then removed, and the remainder (if any) is added to the friendly <color=white>Influence Markers</color> to make up the difference.

The Space Race

The Space Race track contains a marker for each Superpower. Operations points may be spent by a player to attempt to move their marker to the next box on the track. A player may discard one card per turn in an attempt to advance the Space Race, unless a special exception allows additional attempts. The discarded card's Operations value must be equal to or greater than the number shown on the track into which you are attempting to advance. The game will roll the die, and if the number is within the range listed in the target box on the Space Race track, will move your marker to the new box.

Advancing the Space Race track will result in an award of Victory Points, a special ability, or both. The first player to reach a given Space Race box receives the left number of Victory Points, and the second player receives the right number of Victory Points. Special abilities are granted to the first player to reach certain Space Race boxes. The special effect is immediately cancelled when the second player reaches that box.

Events
Operations

A player may play a card as an Event instead of Operations. If the Event is associated with their own Superpower, or is associated with both Superpowers, it takes effect as directed by the card’s text. Some Event cards have an underlined title, and this indicates that the effect of those Events last for the duration of the game. Defcon Status & Military Operations

By the end of each turn, a player needs to have a certain number of <color=white>Military Operations</color>. Failure to do so results in a <color=white>Victory Point</color> penalty. The number of <color=white>Military Operations</color> required each turn is equal to the current DEFCON status number. <color=white>Coup</color> attempts and War Events are <color=white>Military Operations</color>, and when played the game moves the player's marker on the <color=white>Military Operations</color> track a number of spaces equal to the <color=white>Operations</color> value of the card.
Defcon

The DEFCON status measures nuclear tension in the game. It can go down or up due to events and actions by the players, but if at any point it decreases to 1, the game ends immediately. The player responsible for the status marker moving to DEFCON 1 loses the game. Any <color=white>Coup</color> attempt in a <color=white>Battleground</color> country degrades the DEFCON status one level. The consequences of the DEFCON status level will affect a player's ability to perform <color=white>Coup</color> or <color=white>Realignment</color> rolls in specific regions. At the beginning of any turn in which the DEFCON status is lower than 5, the DEFCON status will improve by 1.
Military Operations

By the end of each turn, each player must have played a certain number of <color=white>Military Operations</color>. Failure to do so results in a <color=white>Victory Point</color> penalty. The number of <color=white>Military Operations</color> required each turn is equal to the current DEFCON status number. <color=white>Coup</color> attempts and War Events are <color=white>Military Operations</color>, and when played the game will move the the player's marker on the <color=white>Military Operations</color> track a number of spaces equal to the <color=white>Operations</color> value of the card.
China

The China Card does not count towards the hand limit. When The China Card is played, it is immediately handed to your opponent face down. It may not be played again by your opponent this turn. At the end of the turn, it is flipped face up, ready to be played. To receive the China Card's +1 bonus to Operations, all points must be spent in Asia or Southeast Asia. Play of The China Card can never be compelled by events or a shortage of cards during the action rounds.
Scoring
End Game

The object of the game is to score Victory Points through geographic influence over the six Regions. Each Region has its own "Scoring Card". Playing a Scoring Card causes Victory Points to be scored on how much influence each superpower has in that region at the time the card is played. The Victory Points are totaled for both players, and the net difference is marked on the Victory Point Track. A player may not hold a Scoring Card in their hand at the end of theirturn, as doing so results in automatically losing the game. A player may not be forced to hold a Scoring Card through the effects of a game event.

Scoring Card have the following scoring criteria:

> Presence: A superpower has Presence in a Region if it Controls at least one (1) country in that Region.

> Domination: A superpower has Domination in a Region if it Controls more countries than an opponent and it Controls more Battleground countries in that Region. A superpower must Control at least one (1) non-Battleground and one (1) Battleground country in that Region to achieve domination.

> Control: A superpower has Control of a Region if it Controls more countries in that Region than its opponent, and Controls all of the Battleground countries in that Region.

> Additional Scoring: A +1 VP is granted per country that is under Control and adjacent to the enemy superpower.

> Additional Scoring: A +1 VP is granted per Battleground Country that is under a player's Control in the scoring region.
Victory

The Victory Track shows the ebb and flow of scoring over the course of the game. The first superpower to achieve a net positive twenty (20) Victory Point scores the victory. The game starts at zero (0) Victory points per superpower, and when a player scores a victory point it is added to the Victory Track. Victory Points added to the track either increase the player's Victory Point total, or reduce the opponent's total by the same ammount.

In addition to the Victory Point Track a player may achieve victory by Controlling Europe when it is scored. Additionally, a player will win instantly if their opponent causes the DEFCON level to reach 1, triggering nuclear war. If neither side has achieved victory of any kind by the end of turn 10, every Region except Southeast Asia is then scored. All Regions are calculated before final Victory Points are applied. The player that has accrued the most Victory Points is declared the winner. If a player Controls Europe at this time then they win regardless of the Victory Points. If the net score is a Zero (0), the game is declared a draw.

The Chinese Civil War Space

<margin-right=8.5em>The Chinese Civil War game space is considered to be adjacent to the Soviet Union, and only the Soviet Union. The space is considered to be in Asia, but not in South East Asia. It does not affect any Scoring Card. The only action that may be taken on the Chinese Civil War space is the placement of <color=white>Influence Points</color> by the Soviet player. The US player may not use Operations or Events of any kind to affect the Chinese Civil War space. Once the Soviet player has placed </margin><color=white>3 Influence Points</color> on the Chinese Civil War space, it has no further effect. The markers may be returned to the Soviet player’s pool, and the Chinese Civil War space is ignored for the remainder of the game.
Control

The Soviet player must place 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space to Control it. Soviet Influence is placed in the Chinese Civil War space according to the rules for placing Influence in countries. If the China Card remains unclaimed throughout the game, no player receives the Victory Point for possession of the China Card during end game scoring.
Impact of Control

Until the Soviet Player has placed 3 Influence Points on the Chinese Civil War space, the China Card is not in any player’s possession. Once the Soviet player has placed 3 Influence Points into the space, the player immediately receives the China Card face up and ready for play. Additionally, the ban on play of the Red Scare/Purge and Formosan Resolution events are immediately lifted.

For those of you who would like to dive right into the <color=white>post-Quagmire era</color> and try out the cool possibilities of a Landed Eagle, Star Wars, Chernobyl, Aldrich Ames, the Iranian Hostage Crisis, and Terrorism, here’s a scenario that cuts to the chase.

The Late War period begins in 1975, around, the Fall of Saigon. It is that date in time that has been selected to set the influence and events for the opening of the Late War Scenario. The Late War scenario allows the player to begin a game in that era, playing with the cards that are based off of the events of that time.

The US appears to begin the post-Vietnam era in a decidedly strong position in game turns. Whether or not the dominoes have fallen, the US still dominates Asia, for example. Play of the scenario has shown that a US Automatic Victory is well within reach, so the Soviet player in this scenario wins just for engineering a more graceful decline of the Socialist experiment.

The Turn Zero expansion is a way to freshen up your Twilight Struggle experience. It represents a series of variants on the end of World War II and its aftermath that could have resulted in a substantially different Cold War.

Warning: due to the large number of new possibilities in the starting setup, game balance is not guaranteed with Turn Zero!

Turn Zero defaults to playing without the Chinese Civil War variant and the optional cards from the first Deluxe edition. If you wish to use the Chinese Civil War variant, select the Chinese Civil War Option on the Game Create screen. The Chinese Civil War crisis card is removed before creating the crisis deck (see below), and each player has one Statecraft card discarded at random prior to resolving Crises. This discard is face down, so the players do not know which Statecraft card the opponent discarded.

Turn Zero consists six Crisis cards, ten Statecraft cards, and two modified event cards (Europe Scoring and Nationalist China) The Statecraft cards are divided between the players—each will get the three that are marked with their superpower’s flag.
Procedure

1. Determine sides. Bidding for sides is not recommended when using this variant; however, if bidding is being used, bid and assign sides per the bidding rule you are using. If Influence bidding is not being used, determine sides as you normally would.
2. Each player should now receive their five Statecraft cards.

3. The six Crisis cards are separated into two piles of three each. The first pile contains V-E Day, Yalta and Potsdam, and 1945 Election. The second contains Israel, V-J Day, and Chinese Civil War. Chinese Civil War is not included if you are playing with the Chinese Civil War variant from the first deluxe edition.  The piles are shuffled.
4. The first Crisis card from the first pile is revealed.
Introduction
5. Each player now selects one of their Statecraft cards to modify the Crisis card results.
6. Your opponent's Statecraft card is revealed.

7. Roll a die. Any modifiers from the Statecraft cards (if any) are applied. Cross-reference the result on the face-up Crisis card, and the indicated effects (if any) are implement in the game. We recommend placing bonus Influence in or near the areas on the map where it will go.

Note that the Statecraft cards that give modifiers can only be used once; the dummy cards can be used multiple times.
8. Steps 4-7 are repeated for the rest of the cards in the first pile; then again for the cards in the second pile.
8.1 Once all of the Crisis cards have been resolved, Statecraft cards play no further role in the game and are removed from play.

8.2 Modifications are applied to the event deck as indicated by Crisis results, e.g. the ‘6’ result from 1945 UK General Election. Where a Crisis result indicates that a card’s event has no effect, it remains in the deck and is removed normally should its event be triggered. The event simply does nothing when triggered.
9. If either of the Yalta and Potsdam results that grant choice of a card for the starting hand was rolled, the applicable player now chooses that card.
10. Cards are now dealt. Any card added from step 10 counts as a dealt card—that is, it counts against the starting hand size as if it had been dealt normally.

11. Normal setup is now conducted, with the players placing Influence on the board per the standard setup rules, and modified by the results of the Crises. All extra influence granted from Crises is in addition to that normally received in setup; all influence reduction is taken from that normally received in setup.

Twilight Struggle is a two-player game that simulates the forty-five year dance of intrigue, espionage, political alliances and conflict between the Soviet Union and the United States, known as The Cold War. The nations of the world are the stage, as each country vies to spread their ideology and culture around the globe.
